title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI’s natural gas ambitions
content:
SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big.
Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess.
That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed.
The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects.
“SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva, told TechCrunch via email.
The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s. As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him.
Now, that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless.
The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered.
“This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said.
The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar.
As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics, told the Equity podcast Wednesday.
In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use.
Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected.
SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling.

report.summary: SoftBank’s $7.1B quarterly loss, driven by overordered gas turbines, signals AI’s natural-gas power boom may be hitting a costly ceiling.
report.background: AI data centers have created enormous electricity demand, but grid connection queues now stretch into the early 2030s. Natural gas became a favored stopgap because it is familiar, dispatchable, and faster to deploy than new grid infrastructure. SoftBank, under Masayoshi Son, tried to turn that bottleneck into an advantage: its SB Energy subsidiary announced a $33 billion, 9.2-gigawatt gas plant and reportedly placed nonrefundable deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines—roughly 50% more than needed—to secure scarce equipment early. The strategy echoed SoftBank’s habit of making supersized bets. But turbine overordering carried hidden risk: if AI power demand evolved differently, those deposits could become stranded costs. The loss shows how quickly energy-market optimism can turn into expensive price discovery.
key_points: SoftBank reportedly ordered more than 13 gigawatts of gas turbines, almost 50% above its needs, and paid nonrefundable deposits to jump turbine queues. The move was meant to secure scarce equipment and give SB Energy leverage over AI’s power-hungry data center buildout.

SoftBank posted a $7.1 billion quarterly loss, with more than half tied to power-generating equipment. Over $3 billion reflected deposits the company now considers largely worthless—a costly lesson in speculative procurement during an infrastructure rush.

AI’s electricity demand caught the energy industry off guard, pushing turbine queues into the 2030s. Natural gas looked like a reliable “security blanket,” but it still carries risks such as winter supply curtailments and demand spikes that can raise costs or disrupt operations.

Analysts suggest grid connections plus large batteries may be more cost-effective than building dedicated gas plants. Batteries can shave peak loads and help data centers ride out utility curtailment requests, possibly slowing the gas market’s growth more than SoftBank expected.

The loss is unlikely to trigger mass cancellations of gas plants because AI power demand remains too large. Natural gas is still riding high, but SoftBank’s misstep may mark a practical ceiling for speculative overordering and gas-centric AI power strategies.
report.impact: For the AI industry, SoftBank’s loss is a warning that power procurement is now a major financial risk, not just an engineering detail. Hyperscalers and data center developers may become more cautious about speculative turbine orders and nonrefundable deposits, favoring grid connections, battery storage, and diversified supply contracts. Turbine manufacturers still hold leverage because queues remain long, but overordering could create stranded costs and distort demand signals. For developers, the lesson is to model actual power needs carefully and avoid treating natural gas as a guaranteed shortcut. For regular users, the episode could affect AI service costs, data center siting, and local electricity prices if utilities and operators shift toward grid upgrades and storage rather than dedicated gas plants.
report.tools: To follow AI-data-center power strategy, watch power-system modeling tools such as PyPSA, distribution simulation with GridLAB-D, and energy management via OpenEMS. Electricity Maps and WattTime help track grid carbon intensity and load flexibility; Ascend Analytics and Noreva provide commercial market analysis on gas, batteries, and grid constraints. These tools help readers evaluate whether grid connections, batteries, or gas generation make sense for specific data-center loads.
